cards.text: Pull up a stool, friend. The word of the LORD comes to Jonah son of Amittai, a prophet from Gath-hepher (2 Kings 14:25). And this is NOT small talk.
God tells Jonah to get up, go to the great city of Nineveh, and preach against it. Big city. BIG job.

cards.question: God is sending Jonah to preach against Nineveh. What reason does God give?

answers.text: Its wickedness has come up before Him
Its king has turned his back on Him
Its people have mocked all His prophets

cards.question: Jonah gets up and heads straight for Nineveh, just like God said.

cards.text: Nope. Jonah gets up to flee from the presence of the LORD, goes down to Joppa, and finds a ship, which is like dodging your boss's call and then buying a plane ticket so they can't call again.

cards.question: Jonah has found a ship at Joppa. Where is it bound?

cards.text: So Jonah pays the fare and sails off, away from the presence of the LORD. Friend, the man PAID to run from God.

cards.question: With Jonah out at sea, the LORD hurls a great ___ upon the sea.

cards.text: Such a violent storm comes up that the ship is in danger of breaking apart. I spent YEARS in a junk drawer, friend, and even I'd rather be back in there than on that boat.

cards.question: The sailors are afraid, and each one cries out to his own god.
Next, the sailors throw something into the sea to lighten the load. What is it?
While the sailors work up top, Jonah has gone down to the lowest part of the ship, where he lies down in a deep ___.

cards.text: ASLEEP. The ship is breaking apart, everybody's crying out to their gods, and Jonah is down there like he hit the snooze button on a hurricane.

cards.question: The captain comes to Jonah and tells him to get up and call upon his God.

cards.text: The captain says, “Perhaps this God will consider us, so that we may not perish.” Friend, when the captain is asking YOUR God for help, it is not your day.
Back up top, the sailors want to find out who's responsible for this calamity. Everybody's looking at everybody.

cards.question: How do the sailors find out who's responsible for the storm?
The sailors cast lots, and the lot falls on Jonah.

cards.text: Of COURSE it lands on Jonah. Now the sailors fire off five questions about who's to blame, his work, where he's from, his country and his people, like a job interview in the middle of a storm.

cards.question: Jonah tells the sailors he's a Hebrew who worships the LORD. How does he describe the LORD?

answers.text: The God who made the sea and the dry land
The God who rules from the temple in Jerusalem
The God who led Israel out of the land of Egypt

cards.text: Hold up. Jonah is running from the God who made the sea, and his getaway plan is a BOAT.

cards.question: Jonah has told the sailors he's fleeing from the presence of the LORD, and now they're even more afraid.

cards.text: “What have you done?” they ask him. Meanwhile, the sea keeps growing worse and worse.

cards.question: The sailors ask Jonah what they must do to him to calm the sea. What does Jonah tell them?

cards.text: Then Jonah says, “For I know that I am to blame for this violent storm that has come upon you.” Give the man this much: he owns it.

cards.question: The sailors throw Jonah overboard as soon as he tells them to.

cards.text: Nope. They row HARD to get back to dry land, but the sea rages against them more and more.

cards.question: Out of options, the sailors cry out to the LORD. What do they ask Him?

answers.text: Not to charge them with innocent blood
To carry them safely on to Tarshish
To forgive them for casting the lots

cards.question: The sailors pick Jonah up and cast him into the sea, and the raging sea grows ___.

cards.text: Calm. Friend, I've waited longer for an oven to cool off.

cards.question: With the sea calm, the men ___ the LORD greatly and make ___ to Him.

cards.text: They offer a sacrifice to the LORD too. As for Jonah, he's in the sea, and trust me, friend, this story is NOT done.

findings.problem: The comparison doesn't hold together. Buying a plane ticket doesn't stop a boss from calling, so the punchline 'so they can't call again' makes a reader stop and ask 'huh?' The core action is running far away from the one who gave the order. The joke needs one everyday image with that same action, such as dodging the boss's call and then buying a plane ticket to get away.

rule.text: It clicks instantly for any adult, with no explaining. If a stranger would say "huh?", rewrite it.

findings.problem: "The ship is breaking apart" stretches the text. Jonah 1:4 says the ship was "in danger of breaking apart." Also, "everybody's crying out to their gods" counts in Jonah, but Jonah 1:5 says only the sailors cried out while Jonah was asleep. These are stated as facts, not as part of the joke.

rule.text: Don't stretch the text. Exaggerate only in his own jokes.

findings.problem: The joke's setup, "when the captain is asking YOUR God for help," says the captain is the one asking Jonah's God. In Jonah 1:6, the captain tells Jonah to get up and call upon his God himself. The captain only hopes that this God will consider them.

rule.text: Papa Dorin can retell in his own words and fill in what the text clearly implies. Scene-setting details are fine. He never says anything the text shows is wrong.

findings.problem: The question types in Stop 2 follow a fixed pattern. Cards 2, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11 and 13 alternate multiple choice and true or false seven times in a row: MC, TF, MC, TF, MC, TF, MC. The two fill in the blank cards then come back to back at the end.

rule.text: No formula. Which question type comes next, the order the types come in and where a blank falls are chosen naturally for each card. They never follow a pattern. No stop repeats another stop's pattern, and no type dominates a stop by a wide margin.

findings.problem: The card states a fact from outside the passage, that Jonah was a prophet from Gath-hepher, and gives the reference inline as (2 Kings 14:25). The card's verses field cites only Jonah 1:1. The docs allow outside facts with their reference. They don't say whether that reference goes inline in the card text, goes in the verses field, or both. A single hyphen range can't hold Jonah 1:1 and 2 Kings 14:25 together.
findings.question: When a story card uses a fact from outside the passage, where does its reference go: inline in the text, in the card's verses field, or both? If it goes in the verses field, what format should be used for references to two different books?
